MP003.note: Human platelet / cardiovascular effects of nanoplastics — human health is out of scope for all projects.

reasons.P1: MP concentrations (~39 particles/L, mostly PET fibres, FTIR-confirmed) in ten bottled-water brands — reference values for P1, although the size data are coarser than P1's 1–20 µm target.
Raman counts of MPs down to 1 µm in bottled and tap water with blank and recovery correction; 98% of particles were <20 µm — reference values and a QA/QC approach for P1's 1–20 µm method (Aims 2–3).

reasons.P2: Archived sediment cores from Great Bay Estuary: MP occurrence (~116 particles/g) and a decadal accumulation trend; hydrodynamic modelling shows bed shear stress controls where MPs settle — estuary deposition for P2 Aim 2.

MP005.note: Toxicity of MP chemicals to Daphnia — an effects study; none of the projects covers biological effects.

reasons.P2: Field survey of an urban river near Vienna: MP deposition in sediments is controlled by sedimentary facies and season (backwater deposits up to ~15,500 MP/kg) — directly informs P2 Aim 2 (deposition hotspots).

MP060.note: Biochar offsets MP effects on sugarcane in soil — a soil-amendment study, explicitly out of P3 scope.

reasons.P2: Flume experiments with 3D particle tracking give a transport-stage phase diagram for MP rolling, saltation and suspension — input for P2 Aim 2 transport models.

reasons.P1: SNAP workflow: silicon-nitride nanomembranes concentrate drinking-water particles for optical, electron and Raman analysis on one substrate — candidate sample-prep and identification approach for P1 (Aims 1–2).

Meta-analysis showing grab vs net sampling, sample volume and mesh size shift measured concentrations by orders of magnitude, with contamination the largest bias — informs P1 sampling, blanks and QA/QC (Aims 1 and 3).
reasons.P2: Warns against comparing river and lake concentrations across surveys that used different sampling methods — directly affects how P2 designs and compares field surveys (Aim 2).

reasons.P3: Iron-modified sewage-sludge biochar removed up to 96% of nanoplastics; structural equation modelling ranks capture mechanisms (electrostatic 53%, H-bonding, pores, π–π) — P3 Aims 1–2.

MP009.note: Coastal marine survey around Japan (not estuaries) — P2 excludes marine areas away from estuaries.

reasons.P1: Produces photo-aged, 'true-to-life' MP test materials (PS, PP, LDPE, PVC, PET) characterised by FTIR/NIR — realistic reference particles for P1 validation (Aim 3).

MP013.note: Its abstract says realistic aged particles are needed for 'assessing remediation pathways', so P3 (testing biochar on realistic particles) is defensible; photo-ageing makes P2 defensible.

reasons.P2: Review of streambed pollution sources and impacts that names plastics as a major physical pollutant of urban streambeds — context for P2 deposition work (Aim 2).

MP043.note: Broad multi-stressor review; microplastics are only one part.

reasons.P3: Field test of stormwater filter socks: rice-husk biochar removed ~98% of tyre-wear particles on first use (85% on reuse), outperforming woodchips, especially for particles <100 µm — P3 Aims 2–3.
reasons.P2: Measures tyre-wear particle concentrations in urban stormwater runoff during storms (first-flush peaks) — the input pathway P2 tracks (Aim 1).
Systematic review of MP occurrence, polymers and sources in Asian rivers (2011–2024) — background and comparison data for P2 field surveys (Aims 1–2).

MP014.note: Also reviews sampling and identification methods, so P1 is defensible.

reasons.P1: FT-IR spectral-imaging pipeline (image/tile/spectral corrections + cluster-centroid library matching) that improves polymer identification accuracy and speed — P1 Aim 2.

MP012.note: Bio-based nanoplastics reduce the filtration rate of a freshwater clam — 'filtration' here is the animal's feeding, not capture by a material.

MP018.note: MP transport by ocean surface waves — 'transport' sounds like P2, but it is open-ocean physics.

MP059.note: Biochar + polystyrene MPs, but the target is cadmium adsorption in water and soil. Nothing captures MPs.

MP017.note: Additive-enriched MPs and soil invertebrates — soil and biological effects; out of scope for all projects.

MP019.note: Educational Nile Red counting of 1–5 mm particles in soil — large particles in soil, out of P1 scope.

MP016.note: Global ocean model of fragmentation and transport — open ocean / gyres, out of P2 scope.

MP058.note: Biochar + microplastics, but the biochar captures phosphorus and ammonium; the MPs only change nutrient uptake. Nothing captures MPs.

MP020.note: Captures MPs from water — but with chitosan-coated loofah, not biochar. P3 is biochar only.

reasons.P1: EasyMP reference materials (10–100 µm fragments, 50–1000 µm fibres) with tested homogeneity — usable for spike-recovery and validation in P1 Aim 3.

MP023.note: Reference particles could also be used to test biochar capture efficiency, so P3 is defensible.

MP024.note: MP removal in wastewater treatment — but with chemical coagulants (alum, ACH), not biochar. P2 (effluent loads) is defensible but not expected.

reasons.P1: Backscatter polarimetry + CNN identifies PE/PP particles directly in water (83% accuracy) — an alternative identification approach for P1 Aim 2; transfer to 1–20 µm particles is uncertain.

reasons.P3: Nano-ferric-loaded magnetic biochar removed >90% of PET microfibres from simulated wastewater over pH 4–9 and kept >95% after four regeneration cycles — P3 Aims 1–2.

MP053.note: Targets wastewater effluent, so P2 (effluent inputs) is defensible.

reasons.P2: Development-length expression and regime map for buoyant and sinking plastics in open-channel flow — riverine transport modelling for P2 Aim 2.

reasons.P1: Raman tweezers trap and identify individual sub-micron particles in liquid — a route to the <5 µm fraction that P1 targets (Aim 2).
reasons.P2: Applied to tyre and road wear particles, which reach waters through stormwater runoff — a measurement tool for P2's tyre-wear source (Aim 1).

reasons.P1: Sample-based subsampling for QCL infrared imaging estimates particle and MP counts with bounded error — reduces analysis time for filters with many particles (P1 Aims 2–3).

reasons.P2: Field method quantifying fragmentation of tagged PET bottles during river transport (median ~0.8% mass loss per year) — breakdown of plastics into MPs, P2 Aim 3.

MP028.note: About macroplastics, but explicitly measures fragmentation in rivers.

reasons.P1: Reviews detection techniques — microscopy, mass spectrometry, flow cytometry, FT-IR microscopy, Raman — for micro- and nanoplastics (P1 Aim 2).
reasons.P3: Reviews removal technologies including biochar immobilisation alongside filtration, coagulation and degradation — context for P3.

MP051.note: Broad review covering detection, fate and removal. The fate section makes P2 defensible, but it is not about river transport.

MP026.note: Digestion method for MPs in marine mussel tissue — a method paper, but for a marine organism, not a water matrix.

reasons.P2: UV, heat and mechanical shear in suspension fragment PET, nylon and PAN into micro- and nanoplastics over 12 weeks, quantifying size reduction and nanoplastic formation — fragmentation processes for P2 Aim 3.

MP045.note: The biological test uses human cells, which no project covers; the fragmentation process is what matters for P2. Raman/LDIR characterisation makes P1 defensible.

reasons.P3: Review linking surface properties of biochar, activated carbon, CNTs and graphene to MP removal from wastewater; modified biochar performs well — P3 Aim 2 (mechanisms).

MP027.note: Robot detecting visible particles on beach sand with NIR — marine beach and large particles; out of P1 and P2 scope.

reasons.P3: Magnetic iron-oxide–biochar composite removed ~98.5% of biodegradable PHBV microplastics from simulated secondary effluent, with magnetic separation and reuse — P3 Aims 1–2.

MP054.note: Targets secondary effluent, so P2 is defensible. Note the MPs are a biodegradable polymer.

reasons.P2: Flood type controls plastic deposition on floodplains of two Dutch rivers (obstruction vs low-energy deposition) — deposition processes for P2 Aim 2.

MP032.note: Covers plastics in general (mostly larger items), not only MPs.

reasons.P1: Compares Nile Red and DCVJ fluorescent dyes for detecting micro- and nanoplastics, including false positives from dye aggregation — identification and QA/QC for P1 (Aims 2–3).

MP033.note: Mutation rates in midges exposed to road-runoff sediment — a biological-effects study. Tyre wear + stormwater may tempt P2/P3, but nothing is transported or captured.

reasons.P3: Untreated and air-oxidised biochar in bioretention columns removed 0.02–1 µm polystyrene nanoplastics from synthetic stormwater; vegetation reduced later leaching — P3 Aims 1 and 3.
reasons.P2: Bioretention treats stormwater runoff before it reaches rivers — how well it retains MPs changes urban input loads (P2 Aim 1).

reasons.P1: Nile Red at nanomolar concentration enables single-particle counting of nanoplastics in bottled and tap water while controlling dye-aggregate false positives — P1 Aims 2–3 and drinking-water reference values.

reasons.P2: MP abundance and stage-wise removal efficiencies in three Srinagar treatment plants — effluent load data for P2 Aim 1 (WWTP inputs).

MP040.note: Its low-cost filters use sand + charcoal/activated charcoal. Charcoal is close to biochar but the paper never calls it biochar — P3 is defensible, not expected.

reasons.P3: Review of lignin-derived biochar that analyses adsorption mechanisms for microplastics among other emerging contaminants — feedstock and mechanism context for P3 Aims 1–2.

MP057.note: Microplastics are one of four contaminant classes (with pharmaceuticals, pesticides, PFAS).

MP037.note: MP transport through biofilm-covered porous media (soil/subsurface microfluidics). Biofilm–transport links relate to P2 Aim 2, but the setting is soil/subsurface.

reasons.P3: Bibliometric review of biochar and MPs: in water, fixed columns reach ~95–99% removal and magnetic biochar captures particles down to 1 µm — overview for P3.

MP056.note: About half the review covers biochar in MP-contaminated soil, which is out of scope.

reasons.P2: Review of microbead occurrence in Great Lakes waters, sediments and shorelines plus the authors' St. Lawrence and Ottawa river surveys, with wastewater as the entry route — freshwater occurrence and sources for P2 (Aims 1–2).

MP061.note: Biochar used as a filler inside a biodegradable plastic — no MPs are captured from water.
